whyWrong.B: 2 is the height of the leftmost stack — how many times 11 occurs, not the value itself.
whyWrong.C: 9 is a tick on the axis with no dots above it, so no data point takes that value.

Which statement best compares the standard deviations of scores for these teams?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The standard deviation of scores for team A is less than the standard deviation of scores for team B.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The standard deviation of scores for team A is greater than the standard deviation of scores for team B.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of scores for team A is equal to the standard deviation of scores for team B.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the standard deviations.

whyCorrect: Standard deviation measures how far the values sit from their own mean, so you compare spread, not centre or total. Team A's scores all fall between 25 and 40 and pile up in the middle of that band, while team B's scores run from 20 to 50 with the biggest groups at the two ends and a dip in the middle. Values clustered near the centre give a small standard deviation; values pushed out to both extremes give a large one, so team A's is the smaller.

whyWrong.B: This reverses the comparison. Team A looks taller only because its scores are packed into fewer intervals, and bar height is frequency, not spread.
whyWrong.C: The two distributions have visibly different shapes — one tightly clustered, one spread to both ends — so their standard deviations cannot be equal.
whyWrong.D: The full distribution of both teams is given, which is everything the standard deviation depends on, so it can be compared.

note: Source prints two histograms (Frequency against Score, 20-50 in width-5 bins). Bar heights read off the graph and are approximate, but the question only compares spread, so the comparison is unaffected.

The weight of each object in two groups, A and B, was recorded. The tables show the distributions of weight, in grams, for the objects in groups A and B.
Group A: weight (grams)Number of objects

The mean weight of the objects in group A is equal to 2.1, and the mean weight of the objects in group B is equal to 11.1. Which of the following statements about the standard deviations of weight for the objects in these two groups is true?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The standard deviation of weight for the objects in group A is less than the standard deviation of weight for the objects in group B.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The standard deviation of weight for the objects in group A is equal to the standard deviation of weight for the objects in group B.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The standard deviation of weight for the objects in group A is greater than the standard deviation of weight for the objects in group B.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the standard deviations of weight for the objects in these two groups.

whyCorrect: The two groups cover the same 5-gram width, so what separates them is where the objects sit inside that width relative to their own mean. In group A the two tallest columns are at the far ends, so most objects are about 2 grams away from the mean of 2.1. In group B half the objects are in the single middle interval, right at the mean of 11.1, and only 4 of the 20 are at the ends. Larger typical distance from the mean means a larger standard deviation, so group A's is greater.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the comparison. Group B has the taller single bar, but bar height is how many objects share a weight, not how far apart the weights are.
whyWrong.B: The shapes are different — A is heaviest at both ends, B is heaviest in the middle — so the spreads cannot be equal.
whyWrong.D: The whole distribution of each group is given, and standard deviation depends only on that, so the comparison can be made. The very different means do not block it, because standard deviation measures distance from each group's own mean.

note: Source prints two histograms (Number of objects against Weight, width-1 bins). Converted to equivalent frequency tables; the means quoted in the stem are the book's.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: Two features of the plot decide this without any calculation. The points fall as x increases, so the slope must be negative, which rules out any equation with a positive x coefficient. And near x = 0 the points sit around y = 25, so the constant term has to be close to 25, not 6. Only y = 28 - 6x has both a negative slope and a constant near 25.

whyWrong.A: The coefficient of x is +28, so this model rises steeply; the data falls.
whyWrong.B: The slope is negative, but the constant term 6 puts the line near y = 6 at x = 0, while the data starts around y = 25 there. This is the answer you get by pairing the right sign with the wrong two numbers.
whyWrong.C: Both numbers are the right size but the slope is positive, so the line rises when the data falls.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. What data point has an actual y-value that is 2 less than the y-value predicted by the line of best fit for the corresponding x-value?
whyCorrect: "2 less than predicted" means the point sits 2 units below the line, so start by throwing out every point that lies above it. Only the point at x = 18 is clearly below the line by about two units: the line is at roughly y = 6 there and the point is at y = 4.

whyWrong.A: At x = 2 the line is at about 12.5 and the point is at 12, so it is only about half a unit below.
whyWrong.B: (6, 14) sits above the line, so its actual value is greater than predicted, not less.
whyWrong.C: (10, 12) also sits above the line, by roughly 3 units.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 20 and y from 2 to 16, with a line of best fit running from about (0, 13.5) down to (20, 5). Points approximately (2, 12), (4, 11), (6, 14), (8, 9), (10, 12), (12, 7), (14, 10), (16, 8), (18, 4). Book prints "for corresponding x-value"; read as "for the corresponding x-value".

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices share the same intercept, so only the slope can tell them apart — find how much y climbs per unit of x. The line starts near y = 77 at x = 0 and reaches roughly y = 865 at x = 10, a rise of about 790 over a run of 10, so the slope is about 79.

whyWrong.A: A slope of 0.01 would make the line essentially flat, rising by 0.1 across the whole graph, while the line climbs by hundreds.
whyWrong.B: A slope of 0.79 would take the line from 77 to only about 85 by x = 10 — still visually flat.
whyWrong.C: A slope of 68.9 puts the line at about 766 when x = 10, which is below the 800 gridline; the drawn line is above it there. This is the trap for reading the run as slightly too long or the rise as slightly too short.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 10 and y from 0 to about 900, with a line of best fit from about (0, 77) to (10, 865). Points approximately (1, 90), (3, 280), (4, 490), (6, 620), (8, 710), (9, 690).

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: Read the two ends of the drawn line. It meets the y-axis at about 3.5, which kills any equation with a negative constant, and it reaches about y = 16 when x = 8. That is a rise of about 12.4 over a run of 8, so the slope is roughly 1.55, not 1.8.

whyWrong.A: The intercept is right but a slope of 1.8 would put the line at 3.5 + 14.4 = 17.9 when x = 8, above the top of the graph. Check the far end of the line, not just where it starts.
whyWrong.B: A constant of -2.4 puts the line below the x-axis at x = 0, but the drawn line crosses the y-axis above 3.
whyWrong.D: The slope is negative, so this line falls; the data and the drawn line both rise.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 16, with a line of best fit from about (0, 3.7) to (8, 16). Points approximately (0.3, 4), (0.5, 6), (2, 8), (2.2, 6), (3.3, 10), (3.5, 9), (4.3, 11), (4.5, 10), (5.5, 14), (6.5, 12).

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points fall to a lowest value and then rise again, so the model is a parabola, and the only things to match are where the bottom sits. The lowest points are near x = 0 with y just under 10, so the vertex is at about (0, 8). Writing the vertex form, a parabola with vertex on the y-axis at height 8 is \( y = x^{2} + 8 \).

whyWrong.A: \( y = x^{2} - 8 \) has its vertex at (0, -8), so it would predict negative y-values near x = 0; every plotted point has y above 8.
whyWrong.C: \( y = (x-8)^{2} \) has its vertex at x = 8, off to the right of every point shown, so it would be decreasing across the whole graph instead of turning around near x = 0.
whyWrong.D: \( y = (x+8)^{2} \) has its vertex at x = -8, so it would be increasing across the whole graph. The sign inside the parentheses shifts the curve left or right, not up or down.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: Two readings settle it. The line crosses the y-axis above the origin, at about 3.3, so the constant term is positive. And the line rises as x increases, so the coefficient of x is positive. Only y = 3.3 + 1.6x has both signs positive.

whyWrong.B: This has no x in it at all, so it is the horizontal line y = 1.7. The drawn line is not horizontal.
whyWrong.C: A constant of -3.3 would put the line 3.3 units below the origin at x = 0, but the drawn line starts above the origin.
whyWrong.D: Both signs are wrong: the line would start below the origin and fall, while the drawn line starts above it and rises.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 16, with a line of best fit from about (0, 3.3) up through (8, 16). Points approximately (0.5, 4), (1.8, 6), (2, 8), (2.5, 6), (3.5, 10), (3.5, 7), (5.5, 14), (6.8, 13). Choice B is printed as "y = 3.3 - 1.6", with no x term - reproduced as printed. Stem printed as "best represents the of best fit shown"; read as "the line of best fit".

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, together with a line of best fit. Which of the following is closest to the slope of this line of best fit?
whyCorrect: The line falls from left to right, so the slope is negative straight away, leaving only -3.3 and -1.1. Take the two easiest points on the line: it meets the y-axis at 14 and the x-axis at about 13. That is a drop of 14 over a run of 13, a slope of about -1.1.

whyWrong.A: -3.3 is three times too steep; a line that steep would drop from 14 to 0 in about 4 units of x, not 13.
whyWrong.C: The sign is wrong — a positive slope rises, and this line falls.
whyWrong.D: Wrong sign and roughly three times too steep.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 16 and y from 0 to 16, with a line of best fit from (0, 14) to about (13, 0). Points approximately (3, 10), (5, 10.4), (5.5, 6.4), (6, 9), (7.5, 4.2).

whyCorrect: The points fall as x increases, so the coefficient of x must be negative. That leaves two options, and the constant term is what the model predicts at x = 0, where the data sits at about y = 9 — so the constant is 8.7, not 0.8. The gentle drop from about 9 to about 1 over ten units of x also matches a slope near -0.8, not -8.7.

whyWrong.B: The sign is right but the two numbers are swapped: this line starts at 0.8 and drops to about -77 by x = 9, far off the graph.
whyWrong.C: Correct constant, wrong sign on the slope — this line rises.

whyCorrect: Every plotted x-value is negative and every plotted y-value is positive, and the line falls from left to right, so its slope is negative. Only y = -x + 5.7 has a negative slope, and it also gives sensible values here: at x = -14 it predicts 19.7, which matches the top-left end of the drawn line.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The data falls as x increases, so the coefficient of x is negative — that rules out the two choices with a plus sign. Between the remaining two, the constant is the predicted value at x = 0. Extending the pattern back from (1, 7) gives about 8 or 9 there, so the constant is 8.7. The drop of about 6 units across 9 units of x also matches a slope of -0.8, not -8.7.

whyWrong.A: Positive slope; the line rises while the data falls.
whyWrong.B: Right sign, but the numbers are swapped. A slope of -8.7 would send the line from 0.8 down past -70 by x = 9.
whyWrong.C: Right constant, wrong sign on the slope.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 10 and y from 0 to 10. Points approximately (1, 7), (2, 7), (3, 5), (5, 5), (5.3, 5), (7, 4), (7.5, 4), (9, 2), (9.5, 1). Same four answer choices as Scatterplots question 9 in this book, with different plotted data.

stem: The scatterplot shows the recorded temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, against time, in days since June 1. During which of the following time periods did the greatest increase in recorded temperature take place?
whyCorrect: An increase means the later point is higher than the earlier one, so first discard any interval where the graph goes down. Only two intervals rise: 2 to 3 and 6 to 7. From x = 2 to x = 3 the temperature climbs from about 60°F to about 75°F, a jump of roughly 15 degrees, while from x = 6 to x = 7 it rises only about 2 degrees.

whyWrong.A: This interval does rise, but only from about 62°F to about 64°F — a much smaller increase.
whyWrong.B: From x = 5 to x = 6 the temperature falls, from about 67°F to about 62°F. A large change is not the same as a large increase.
whyWrong.D: From x = 1 to x = 2 the temperature falls from about 69°F to about 60°F. This is the biggest change of all, which is why it is the trap, but it is a decrease.

note: Scatterplot, Temperature (°F) from 0 to 80 against Time (days since June 1) from 1 to 8. Points approximately (1, 69), (2, 60), (3, 75), (4, 68), (5, 67), (6, 62), (7, 64).

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, for the data set P. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. Data set Q is created by adding 540 units to the value of x for each data point from the data set P. Which of the following could be an equation of a line of best fit for the data set Q?
whyCorrect: Sliding every point 540 units to the right shifts the line right by 540 but does not tilt it, so the slope is unchanged and only the constant moves. First get the slope from the graph: the drawn line climbs from about 14.2 at x = 100 to about 14.95 at x = 130, a rise of 0.75 over a run of 30, or about 0.027 — that is \( \frac{35}{1301} \), not \( \frac{1}{131} \approx 0.0076 \). Then apply the shift: replacing x by x - 540 lowers the constant by \( 540 \times \frac{35}{1301} \approx 14.5 \), and the original constant is about 14.2 - 100(0.027) ≈ 11.5, leaving about -3.

whyWrong.B: The slope \( \frac{1}{131} \) is about a third of the slope drawn on the graph, so this line is far too flat whatever its constant is.
whyWrong.C: Same wrong slope as choice B.
whyWrong.D: This has the right slope but the constant has been moved the wrong way. Shifting the data to larger x must decrease the value at x = 0, not raise it by about 14.5.

note: Scatterplot, x from about 95 to 132 and y from 13 to 15.2, with a line of best fit from about (98, 14.2) to (130, 14.95). Points approximately (102, 14.4), (105, 14.6), (108, 14.5), (113, 14.6), (117, 14.8), (118, 14.7), (127, 14.9), (128, 15.0), (130, 15.05). The book prints the choices without a leading "y =".

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points climb at a steady rate — equal steps right produce roughly equal steps up — so the model is linear, not exponential, and it is increasing. That leaves only y = -582 + 1.2x, whose slope of 1.2 matches the roughly one-to-one climb across the graph.

whyWrong.B: The coefficient of x is negative, so this model falls as x grows, while the data rises.
whyWrong.C: An exponential with a negative coefficient in front gives negative y-values for every x; all the plotted points are positive.
whyWrong.D: This grows by a factor of 1.2 for each increase of 1 in x. Over the plotted range, which runs to x = 4,000, that is an unimaginably large number, not 4,000. Exponential growth would also show as a curve that steepens, and these points lie on a straight path.

stem: In the given scatterplot, a line of best fit for the data is shown. Which of the following is closest to the slope of this line of best fit?
whyCorrect: The line falls from left to right, so the slope is negative — that removes both positive choices immediately. For the size, take two points on the line: it starts near (0, 7.5) and reaches about (10, 1), a drop of roughly 6.5 across 10 units of x, so the slope is about -0.65, closest to -0.7.

whyWrong.A: A slope of -7 would drop 7 units for every single unit of x; this line takes the whole width of the graph to drop that far.
whyWrong.C: Right size, wrong sign. A positive slope rises.
whyWrong.D: Wrong sign and about ten times too steep.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 10 and y from 0 to 10, with a line of best fit from about (0, 7.5) to (10, 0.9). Points approximately (0, 6), (1.2, 8), (2.2, 7), (3, 5), (4.5, 4), (5.2, 3), (6.5, 4), (7.2, 2), (8.8, 1), (9.8, 1).

stem: The scatterplot shows the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length in centimeters predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: The question asks what the line predicts, not where a data point sits, so go up from x = 3 to the line rather than to any dot. The line runs from about 88 cm at age 1 to about 135 cm at age 6, climbing roughly 9.4 cm per year, which puts it near 107 cm at age 3. Rounded to the nearest 10 cm that is 110.
note: Scatterplot, body length (cm) 0 to 140 against age (years) 1 to 6, with a line of best fit from about (0.5, 84) to (6, 135). Points approximately (1, 87), (2, 108), (4, 113), (5, 133), (6, 134). The line at x = 3 reads about 107, so the rounded answer is 110; the reading is close to the 105 boundary, so a human should confirm against the printed key. Book prints "of of a New Zealand fur seal"; read as "of a".

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, together with a line of best fit. Which of the following best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices start at 148.13, so only the slope separates them — work out how much y gains per unit of x. The line climbs from about 148 at x = 0 to about 735 at x = 10, a rise of roughly 590 over 10, so the slope is close to 59. The two small slopes can be dismissed on sight, since a slope under 1 would leave the line essentially flat while this line climbs by hundreds.

whyWrong.A: A slope of 0.02 raises y by only 0.2 across the whole graph — a flat line.
whyWrong.B: A slope of 0.59 raises y by about 6 across the whole graph, still flat at this scale.
whyWrong.C: 48.61 is the right order of magnitude but too shallow: it puts the line at about 634 when x = 10, well below where the drawn line ends.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 10 and y from 0 to about 850, with a line of best fit from about (0, 148) to (10.3, 750). Points approximately (1, 120), (2, 340), (4, 420), (5, 390), (6, 550), (7, 510). A least-squares fit to those points gives slope 59.3 and intercept 141, which confirms choice D.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, together with a line of best fit. Which of the following is closest to the slope of the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: The line falls from left to right, so the slope is negative, which leaves -11.19 and -0.84. The line drops from about y = 11 at x = 0 to about y = 4.5 at x = 8, a fall of roughly 6.5 over a run of 8, giving a slope near -0.8.

whyWrong.A: -11.19 is the y-intercept dressed up as a slope. A slope that steep would drop the line 11 units for each single unit of x, taking it off the bottom of the graph before x = 2.
whyWrong.C: Right size, wrong sign — a positive slope rises.
whyWrong.D: Wrong sign and about thirteen times too steep.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 16, with a line of best fit from about (0, 11) to (8, 4.5). Points approximately (1, 10.4), (2, 9.6), (4, 7.5), (5, 6.7), (6, 6.1), (7, 5.3).

stem: In the given scatterplot, a line of best fit for the data is shown. Which of the following equations best represents this line of best fit?
whyCorrect: The drawn line passes through the origin and rises to about (5, 5.2), so it has a positive slope of roughly 1 and no constant term. That is y = 1.1x.

whyWrong.B: A negative slope falls from left to right; this line rises.
whyWrong.C: y = 5.2 has no x in it, so it is the horizontal line at height 5.2. The drawn line is not horizontal — it only reaches 5.2 at the far right.
whyWrong.D: y = -5.2 is a horizontal line below the x-axis, nowhere near the data.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 6 and y from 0 to 6, with a line of best fit from (0, 0) to about (5, 5.15). Points approximately (0, 0), (1, 1.5), (1, 0.8), (2, 1.1), (2.5, 3), (3, 2.9), (3.5, 4), (4, 4.8), (5, 5.15).

stem: The graph models the number of active projects a company was working on x months after the end of November 2011, where 0 ≤ x ≤ 6. According to the model, what is the predicted number of active projects the company was working on at the end of November 2011?
whyCorrect: "At the end of November 2011" is zero months after the end of November 2011, so set x = 0 and read the height of the curve where it meets the y-axis. That value is 8.

whyWrong.A: 0 is the x-value you substitute, not the y-value you read off. The curve does not touch the x-axis anywhere.
whyWrong.C: 11 is the value at x = 2 and again at x = 6, not at x = 0.
whyWrong.D: 12 is the highest point of the curve, reached at x = 4 — the maximum over the whole period, not the starting value.

note: Graph, x from 0 to 6 and y from 0 to 13, a smooth curve rising from (0, 8) through (2, 11) to a maximum at (4, 12) and back down to (6, 11). Book prints the domain as "0 >= x >= 6", which is backwards; read as 0 <= x <= 6.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, together with a line of best fit. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: Only the two signs matter here, since every choice uses the same numbers. The line rises from left to right, so the coefficient of x is positive, and it crosses the y-axis just above the origin at about 0.9, so the constant is positive too.

whyWrong.B: Negative slope — this line would fall.
whyWrong.C: The slope is right but a constant of -0.8 puts the crossing point below the x-axis; the drawn line crosses above it.
whyWrong.D: Both signs wrong: this line starts below the origin and falls.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to 8 and y from 0 to 16, with a line of best fit from about (0, 0.9) to (8, 15.5). Points approximately (0.5, 2), (1.8, 4), (2.5, 6), (2.5, 4), (3.3, 8), (3.8, 5), (4.3, 9), (4.5, 8), (5.5, 12), (6.5, 12).

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, for data set A. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. Data set B is created by subtracting 9 units from the value of y for each data point from data set A. Which of the following is closest to the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the line of best fit for data set B?
whyCorrect: Lowering every y-value by 9 slides the whole line down 9 units without tilting it, so the new intercept is the old intercept minus 9. Get the old one by extending the drawn line back to the y-axis: it passes through roughly (12, 45) and (37, 20), a slope of about -1, so at x = 0 it is near 57 — and the only choice 9 below a value in that region is 45.57. The trap is that the line starts well to the right of the y-axis, so the intercept has to be extrapolated, not read.

whyWrong.B: 53 would require the original line to cross at 62, which is above the top of the plotted y-axis and far above where the drawn line is heading.
whyWrong.C: 59.62 is roughly the original intercept region, so this is the answer you get by forgetting to subtract the 9.
whyWrong.D: 62.75 is higher still, and would need a much steeper line than the one drawn.

note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to about 50 and y from 0 to 60, with a line of best fit through about (12, 45) and (37, 20). Points approximately (12, 45), (13, 45), (15, 42), (16, 41), (17, 39), (22, 32), (25, 30), (28, 24), (29, 31), (30, 25), (33, 30), (36, 20). A least-squares fit to those readings gives intercept 56 and slope -0.97, so the shifted intercept is about 47, nearest to choice A.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. A line of best fit is also shown. Which of the following equations best represents the line of best fit shown?
whyCorrect: Only the two signs differ between the choices. The line rises from left to right, so the coefficient of x is positive, and it meets the y-axis slightly above the origin at about 0.7, so the constant is positive as well.

whyWrong.B: Negative slope — this line falls as x increases.
whyWrong.C: Right slope, but a constant of -0.6 puts the crossing point below the x-axis, while the drawn line crosses above the origin.
whyWrong.D: Both signs wrong.

note: The book labels the fourth choice "C)" as well; recorded here as D. Scatterplot, x from 0 to 9 and y from 0 to 16, with a line of best fit from about (0, 0.7) to (9, 14.8). Points approximately (1, 2), (2, 4), (2, 3), (3, 6), (3, 5), (4, 9), (4, 8), (5, 12), (5, 11), (6, 12), (6, 10), (7, 9).

stem: The scatterplot shows 5 measurements of the body length, in centimeters (cm), of a New Zealand fur seal from an age of 1 year to 6 years old. A line of best fit is also shown. For a New Zealand fur seal at an age of 3 years old, what is the body length predicted by the line of best fit, to the nearest 10 cm?
whyCorrect: Read the line, not the dots — there is no measurement at age 3, which is exactly why the line is there. The line runs from about 68 cm at age 0 to about 126 cm at age 6, gaining roughly 9.7 cm a year, so at age 3 it is near 97 cm. To the nearest 10 cm that is 100.
note: Scatterplot, body length (cm) 0 to 140 against age (years) 0 to 6, with a line of best fit from about (0, 68) to (6, 126). Points approximately (1, 80), (2, 100), (4, 105), (5, 120), (6, 125). Same wording as Scatterplots question 16 in this book but different data, so the two answers differ.

stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y. Which of the following equations is the most appropriate linear model for the data shown?
whyCorrect: The points rise as x increases, so the slope is positive and the two negative choices are out. For the size, compare a point's two coordinates: near x = 9 the value of y is about 10, and near x = 4 it is about 4.5. The y-value stays close to the x-value, so the slope is about 1, not 2.

whyWrong.A: Negative slope, and twice too steep; this line falls below the x-axis for every positive x.
whyWrong.B: Negative slope — the model would fall while the data rises.
whyWrong.D: A slope of 2 predicts y = 18 when x = 9, but the plotted value there is about 10. Doubling is the trap if you only check that the data rises.

stem:
In the figure, parallel lines a and b are intersected by lines c, d, and e. If x = 49, y = 136, and v < z, which statement about x and w must be true?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Look for the two triangles that x and w each sit in. Line c cuts both parallel lines, so the angle it makes with b and the angle it makes with a are equal — and each of those triangles has that same angle, 180 - 136 = 44 degrees, as a second angle. In the triangle containing x, the third angle is v, so x = 180 - 44 - v = 136 - v. In the triangle containing w, the third angle is z, so w = 136 - z by exactly the same count. Since v < z, subtracting the smaller number leaves the larger result, so x > w. (As a check, x = 49 forces v = 87, and z must then exceed 87.)

whyWrong.A: This is the comparison you get by carrying v < z straight through to x and w, but both appear subtracted from 136, which flips the inequality.
whyWrong.C: x = w would require v = z, and the problem states v < z.
whyWrong.D: x + w = 136 - v + 136 - z = 272 - (v + z), which is only 90 if v + z = 182 — nothing in the problem forces that.

note: Figure: two parallel vertical lines, a on the left and b on the right, crossed by three slanted lines. Line d runs down to the right across both, meeting a at the point where v is marked (right of a, below d). Line c runs up to the right across both, meeting b at the point where y is marked (right of b, below c). Lines c and d meet to the right of b at the point where x is marked (the wedge opening rightward). Line e runs down to the right across both, meeting b where z is marked (right of b, below e); c and e meet to the left of a, at the point where w is marked (the wedge opening leftward).

stem: For two acute angles, ∠A and ∠B, \( \cos A = \sin B \). The measures, in degrees, of ∠A and ∠B are x + 8 and 4x + 2, respectively. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: For acute angles, the cosine of one equals the sine of another exactly when the two angles are complementary — that is the meaning of "co-sine". So set the measures to add to 90: (x + 8) + (4x + 2) = 90, giving 5x + 10 = 90 and x = 16. Check: the angles are 24° and 66°, which add to 90°.

whyWrong.A: 37 comes from setting the two angles equal to each other and solving x + 8 = 4x + 2 incorrectly, or from setting the sum to 180 rather than 90. With x = 37 the angles are 45° and 150°, and 150° is not acute.
whyWrong.B: 34 makes the angles 42° and 138°, which sum to 180°, not 90°. Supplementary is the wrong relationship — that is what equal sines would give.
whyWrong.D: 2 makes the angles 10° and 10°. Equal angles would mean sin A = sin B, not cos A = sin B.

stem: For two acute angles ∠Q and ∠R, \( \cos Q = \sin R \). The measures, in degrees, of ∠Q and ∠R are x + 21 and 4x + 9, respectively. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: For acute angles, cosine and sine are equal exactly when the angles are complementary, so the two measures must add to 90. Solve (x + 21) + (4x + 9) = 90: that is 5x + 30 = 90, so x = 12. The angles are then 33° and 57°, which add to 90°.

whyWrong.A: 4 makes the angles 25° and 25°. Equal angles would give sin Q = sin R, not cos Q = sin R.
whyWrong.C: 30 makes the angles 51° and 129°, a sum of 180°. Supplementary is the wrong relationship, and 129° is not acute.
whyWrong.D: 69 makes the angles 90° and 285°, neither of which is acute; it comes from solving x + 21 = 4x + 9 with a sign slip.

stem: The measure of angle R is \( \frac{2\pi}{3} \) radians. The measure of angle T is \( \frac{13\pi}{18} \) radians greater than the measure of angle R. What is the measure of angle T, in degrees?
whyCorrect: Add the two radian measures first, using a common denominator of 18: \( \frac{2\pi}{3} = \frac{12\pi}{18} \), so angle T is \( \frac{12\pi}{18} + \frac{13\pi}{18} = \frac{25\pi}{18} \) radians. Then multiply by \( \frac{180}{\pi} \) to convert: \( \frac{25\pi}{18} \times \frac{180}{\pi} = 25 \times 10 = 250 \) degrees.

whyWrong.A: 120 is angle R alone in degrees; the 13π/18 was never added.
whyWrong.B: 130 is the 13π/18 part alone in degrees; angle R was never added.
whyWrong.D: 500 comes from converting with a factor of 360/π instead of 180/π, or from doubling the correct answer.

stem:
In the figure, two lines intersect at a point. If w = 150, what is the value of z?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The angle marked w is above the crossing point and the angle marked z is below it, so they are vertical angles — opposite each other across the intersection, not side by side. Vertical angles are always equal, so z = 150. The figure not being drawn to scale does not matter; the relationship holds either way.

whyWrong.A: 30 is 180 - 150, which is the size of the two angles at the sides of the crossing. Those are supplementary to w, not equal to it, and z is not one of them.
whyWrong.B: 50 has no basis here; it looks like dividing 150 by 3.
whyWrong.C: 75 is half of 150; nothing in the figure halves the angle.

note: Figure: two straight lines crossing at one point, forming an X. The angle above the crossing is labelled w and the angle below it is labelled z.

stem:
In the figure shown, line r is parallel to line s, and both lines are intersected by line t. If x = 2w + 24, y = 5w + 29, and 7w = a, where a is a constant, what is the value of a?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The marked angles sit on the same side of the transversal, one below it and one above it, at the two parallel lines — so they are co-interior and add to 180, not equal. Write (2w + 24) + (5w + 29) = 180, which gives 7w + 53 = 180 and 7w = 127. The question asks for a = 7w, so you never need w itself: the answer is 127.
note: Figure: two parallel vertical lines, r on the left and s on the right, crossed by a line t that rises to the right. x is marked in the wedge to the left of r and below t; y is marked in the wedge to the left of s and above t.

stem: In the figure, line n intersects lines r and s. Line r is parallel to line s. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both marked angles sit in the same position relative to their intersection — above the horizontal line and to the right of n — so they are corresponding angles. When a transversal crosses parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal, so x = 164. No subtraction from 180 is needed, because the two angles are matching, not adjacent.
note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, r above and s below, crossed by a line n running from upper left to lower right. The 164-degree angle is marked above r and to the right of n; x is marked above s and to the right of n.

stem: In the figure, line n intersects lines r and s. Line r is parallel to line s. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Both marked angles occupy the same corner of their intersection — above the horizontal line and to the left of n — so they are corresponding angles. A transversal cutting parallel lines makes corresponding angles equal, so x = 138. There is nothing to subtract from 180 here, because the two angles are in matching positions rather than side by side.
note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, r above and s below, crossed by a line n rising from lower left to upper right. The 138-degree angle is marked above r and to the left of n; x is marked above s and to the left of n.

stem: The difference between the measure of angle A and the measure of angle B is \( -\frac{3}{4}\pi \) radians. Which expression shows the difference between the measure of angle A and the measure of angle B, in degrees?
whyCorrect: To turn radians into degrees you multiply the whole radian measure by \( \frac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} \), because π radians and 180° are the same angle. The radian measure here is \( -\frac{3}{4}\pi \), all of it, so the expression is \( -\frac{3}{4}\pi \cdot \frac{180^{\circ}}{\pi} \). (It works out to -135°, which is a useful check.)

whyWrong.A: The π from the radian measure has been dropped, so this is \( -\frac{3}{4} \) of \( \frac{180}{\pi} \), about -43°, not -135°.
whyWrong.B: This uses the reverse conversion factor, \( \frac{\pi}{180^{\circ}} \), which turns degrees into radians. It gives about -0.04, far too small.
whyWrong.D: 360° corresponds to 2π radians, not π, so this factor doubles the result to -270°.

stem:
In the figure, parallel lines r and s are intersected by lines t, u, and w. If d = 42, g = 143, and h > d, which statement about j and p must be true?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Both j and p are the third angle of a triangle that has line t as one side, and both triangles borrow the same angle from t. Because r and s are parallel, the angle t makes with each of them is the same, so each triangle contains an angle of 180 - 143 = 37 degrees on that side. The triangle holding j has h as its remaining angle, giving j = 180 - 37 - h = 143 - h; the triangle holding p has d, giving p = 143 - d = 101. Since h > d, more is being subtracted in the first case, so j < p.

whyWrong.A: j = p would require h = d, and the problem states h > d.
whyWrong.B: j + p = (143 - h) + (143 - d) = 286 - (h + d), which equals 90 only if h + d = 196 — nothing given forces that.
whyWrong.C: This carries h > d straight through to j and p, but both are formed by subtracting those angles from 143, which reverses the inequality.

note: DEFECT: the stem names the parallel lines r and s and the transversals t, u, w, but the printed figure labels the two horizontal parallel lines d and e and the three slanted lines a, b, c - and "d" is also used as an angle name in the same figure. Figure as it should read: two horizontal parallel lines, r above and s below. Line t descends from upper left to lower right, crossing r then s. Lines u and w both descend from upper right to lower left; u crosses r to the left of t's crossing and s well to the left, w crosses r well to the right and s just right of t's crossing. Angle j is the upward-opening wedge where t and u meet above r; g is at t's crossing of r, above r and right of t; d is at w's crossing of r, above r and right of w; h is at u's crossing of s, above s and right of u; p is the downward-opening wedge where t and w meet below s.

stem:
In the figure, line p is parallel to line q, and t intersects both of them. What is the value of x + 142?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: The two marked angles sit side by side on the same side of line q, split by the transversal, so together they make the straight angle along q. That means x + 142 = 180 directly — you never have to find x on its own, and the fact that p is parallel to q is not needed at all.

whyWrong.A: 52 is not the sum of anything here; it may come from 142 - 90.
whyWrong.B: 90 would mean the two angles are complementary, but they lie along a straight line, not in a right angle.
whyWrong.C: 142 is one of the two angles; the question asks for their sum, so x is being treated as 0. This is the answer if you read the question as asking only for the marked value.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, p above and q below, crossed by a line t that descends from upper left to lower right. At t's crossing of q, x is marked above q on the left of t and 142 degrees is marked above q on the right of t.

stem: In the figure shown, line m is parallel to line n, and line k intersects both lines. Which of the following statements is true?
whyCorrect: Work from the 135-degree angle, which sits below n on the left of k. The angle marked s is directly opposite it across the crossing point — above n on the right of k — so they are vertical angles and s = 135. Every other marked angle is on the same side of k or the same side of the horizontal line as the 135, which makes it a linear pair instead, worth 45.

whyWrong.A: q is above m on the left of k, which corresponds to the angle above n on the left of k. That one pairs with s along line n, so q = 45.
whyWrong.B: r is vertical to q, so r = 45 as well.
whyWrong.D: t is below n on the right of k, sharing line n with the 135-degree angle. They form a straight angle, so t = 45.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, m above and n below, crossed by a line k descending from upper left to lower right. At k's crossing of m: q is marked above m to the left of k, r below m to the right of k. At k's crossing of n: s is marked above n to the right of k, t below n to the right of k, and 135 degrees below n to the left of k.

stem:
In the figure, line q is parallel to line r, and both lines are intersected by line s. If y = 2x + 9, what is the value of x?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
whyCorrect: Find y first. The 61-degree angle is above q on the right of s, while y is above r on the left of s — opposite sides of the transversal — so they are co-interior rather than corresponding, and y = 180 - 61 = 119. Then solve 119 = 2x + 9, giving 2x = 110 and x = 55.

whyWrong.A: 26 comes from setting y = 61 (treating the two angles as equal) and solving 61 = 2x + 9.
whyWrong.B: 35 comes from 2x + 9 = 79 or a similar slip; no angle in the figure measures 79 degrees.
whyWrong.D: 65 comes from solving 2x + 9 = 139, or from using 180 - 61 = 119 but then dividing before subtracting the 9.

note: Figure: two parallel horizontal lines, q above and r below, crossed by a line s rising from lower left to upper right. The 61-degree angle is marked above q to the right of s; y is marked above r to the left of s.
